title: OpenAI launches MedChemBench: GPT-6.2 Astra scores 84.5% on medicinal chemistry reasoning
summary: Medicinal chemists face the same question every day: which compound to synthesize and test next. OpenAI's new MedChemBench uses 99 problems drawn from published research to test whether AI can connect molecular structures, experimental evidence, and the decision of what to try next. The best-performing model, GPT-6.2 Astra, earned 84.5% of available credit at the xhigh setting, but compound selection and numerical prediction remain weak spots.
ai_summary: OpenAI released MedChemBench on November 20, 2026, a benchmark for medicinal chemistry reasoning. It uses 99 problems drawn from published research to test whether AI can connect molecular structures, experimental evidence, and the next compound to test. At xhigh, the highest shared reasoning setting, GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of available credit, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 83.3% and GPT-5.6 Sol at 58.2%. By component, Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures at 95.4%, but earned only about half the credit on compound selection and numerical prediction. For scientists who want to use AI in drug discovery, this reveals the models' strengths and limits; OpenAI is clear that the results do not show models can discover new drugs, cannot rule out prior exposure to public sources, and each problem was attempted once with no tools or feedback.
brief: MedChemBench contains 99 problems, drawn from 117 papers and patents and covering 761 distinct molecular structures.
At the xhigh setting, total scores were GPT-6.2 Astra 84.5%, GPT-6 Astra 83.3%, GPT-6.1 Sol 82.0%, and GPT-5.6 Sol 58.2%.
Astra earned 95.4% on reconstructing molecular structures, but only about half the credit on compound selection and numerical prediction.
On the 18-atom ring spatial-reasoning problem, GPT-6 Astra got all 10 attempts right; the GPT-5.6 models got all 10 wrong.

sections.h: What MedChemBench is: a test of medicinal chemistry reasoning

blocks.p: OpenAI released MedChemBench on November 20, 2026. It is not itself a drug-discovery AI, but an evaluation set: it checks whether a model can match what a molecule looks like with what experiments measured, then decide which compound to try next. Medicinal chemistry is the field of designing, modifying, and evaluating compounds as potential medicines.

The hardest part of this work is the trade-off: improving one property often makes another worse. A compound can act strongly against a disease-related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. A working medicinal chemist spends their days designing, synthesizing, and testing a series of related compounds, then judging where to go next. MedChemBench is designed to test whether AI has that reasoning ability—connecting structural changes to experimental evidence.

sections.h: What four abilities does it grade?

blocks.p: MedChemBench splits its scoring into four categories. For most problems, the model receives the context available at a chosen point in a research project: the biological target, the research goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings. It is then graded on four dimensions:

list: Molecular structures: assemble molecules from the chemical drawings and groups provided; atom connections and stereochemistry (the spatial arrangement of atoms) must both be correct.
Scientific reasoning: explanations must be supported by the evidence provided, such as why one compound was chosen over another.
Ranking and selection: compound rankings and choices must meet the stated requirements.
Property prediction: predicted values and categories must be close to the results reported in the source literature, including measured and calculated properties.

sections.h: How to read the scores: who earned what

blocks.p: At xhigh, the shared setting with the highest reasoning effort—a mode that lets models think more—the top total came from GPT-6.2 Astra at 84.5% of available credit, followed by GPT-6 Astra at 83.3%, GPT-6.1 Sol at 82.0%, GPT-6.1 Terra at 75.1%, and GPT-5.6 Sol at 58.2%.

blocks.p: The 84.5% figure is the share of available credit, not a simple percentage of correct answers—some problems award partial credit, with scores increasing as predictions get closer to the measured values. Results also change with the reasoning setting: GPT-6 Astra reaches 83.8% at max effort. Figure 2 in the original plots 9 models and 51 model-by-reasoning-setting combinations; the horizontal axis is output tokens, and the trend is that more reasoning raises scores, though clear gaps between models remain.

sections.h: A hard example: inhibit the target, and still be absorbed and not metabolized too quickly

blocks.p: One MedChemBench problem comes from research on PRMT5 inhibitors. PRMT5 is a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. Given molecular structures and results from earlier experiments, the model must predict three properties for three related compounds: how strongly each blocks PRMT5 in cells, how readily it crosses a cell barrier, and how quickly liver enzymes break it down in an assay.

The problem withholds the later experiments, which revealed a trade-off: compound 23 blocks PRMT5 at a lower concentration, but compound 24 crosses the cell barrier more readily and breaks down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay. In other words, no single compound wins on all three. That is the central challenge in medicinal chemistry—being stronger against the target does not mean better permeability or slower breakdown.

Grading checks whether the model reconstructs the molecular structures correctly and how close its predictions are to the measured values; the closer they are, the more partial credit. Measurements already given in the problem must also be reproduced correctly.

sections.h: Before reasoning, models have to draw the molecule correctly

blocks.p: Before discussing properties, a model must first identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry, and MedChemBench checks whether the model preserves that information when reconstructing a molecule.

One problem asks the model to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At xhigh, GPT-6 Astra got all ten responses right; GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna failed all ten. In the examples, GPT-5.6 Sol built a 15-atom ring, and GPT-5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected pieces. These mistakes change the identity of the molecule being analyzed.

This is also Astra's most reliable area: at xhigh it earned 95.4% of available credit on the structure component. By contrast, it scored only about half on compound selection and numerical prediction. In other words, the model reads molecules and explains reasoning well, but it still has a long way to go in choosing the next compound and getting the numbers right.

list: Whether MedChemBench's problem set and scoring scripts are fully available for download: the original only links the paper, with no release date or access details.
Whether the benchmark will become an external OpenAI product or API: the original doesn't say.
How other companies' models perform: this round evaluated only 11 GPT models and listed no external models for comparison.
Whether model training data includes these papers and patents: OpenAI says it cannot rule out that models have seen these public sources before.
Whether these scores reflect real-world drug-discovery ability in the lab: OpenAI says the results don't establish that models can discover new drugs or improve experimental decisions.
Whether each answer was a single attempt with no tools: the original says each response was a single attempt, with no tools, feedback, or new experiments.

blocks.p: Value: for teams in medicinal chemistry or computational chemistry, or anyone wondering whether AI can now help choose compounds, MedChemBench offers a relatively concrete four-part scorecard—molecular structures, scientific reasoning, ranking and selection, and property prediction broken out separately, which is more useful than a single overall number.

Cost: it tests reasoning on historical literature, not real drug-discovery workflows; the problems may have been seen by the models, and every answer is a single attempt with no tools. Treating it as proof that AI can replace chemists would substantially overstate it.

list: If you're a medicinal chemistry researcher: treat it as a capability map, and pay particular attention to the weak spots in selection and property prediction.
If you're on an AI team or building evaluations: the 'strong structure and reasoning, weak selection and prediction' breakdown is a useful starting point for later improvements and comparisons.
If you only want to know whether AI will find new drugs soon: the safer conclusion is not yet. These results show reasoning is improving, not that AI can discover new drugs.
